comment: The folder and flag divide the footer into two recognizable fields, apart from the scheduled time and tags. Tomorrow and Yesterday scan quickly, but the exact deadline is small and populated fields have no explicit edit cue.

Each field has its own chevron even when empty, and the long project fits on one line. The flag and bottom-row position distinguish the deadline from 10:00 AM, but the numeric date takes longer to interpret and the two rows add height.

The folder and flag each have a full-width row and chevron, including when empty. The long project fits on one line. The two rows add height, and only the flag distinguishes “Add date” from setting a scheduled date. Red is the only cue that the populated deadline is overdue.

The divided footer separates the folder from the flag and keeps both apart from the tags and 10:00 AM. “Tomorrow” and “Yesterday” make urgency easy to scan even when the project wraps. The exact date is small, and the populated values lack the edit cue supplied by “Add project” and “Add date” in the empty states.

The folder and flag sit apart from the tags and 10:00 AM schedule. Tomorrow and Yesterday make the deadline easy to scan, but the exact time is small and the dotted divider is the main cue that each half can be edited.

Separate chevrons identify both edit targets even when one field is empty, and the long project fits on one line. The two rows add height, and the flag is the only cue that Oct 17 is a deadline rather than another scheduled time.
Folder and chevron establish the project above the title. The October tile separates the deadline from 10 AM, though the filled tile has a weaker edit cue than “Set due date.”
“in Studio” links the task to its project and “Due in 26h” names the deadline. The wrapped underlined path is harder to skim and the countdown looks like status text.
The folder breadcrumb and explicit due countdown are easy to tell apart. The existing deadline has a vertical rule but no obvious editing control.
The initial and chevron separate Studio from the left-hand tags, but the initial could denote a person. Seven small dates compete with the flagged deadline.
“Filed in” and “Move…” give the footer a clear purpose even for a long path. The date tile above it is prominent but gives little indication it can be changed.
The calendar tile makes the deadline easy to find without squeezing the title. The initial beside Studio has less obvious project meaning until a parent path or “Choose project” appears.
The folder tab comfortably fits the entire project path. The week strip gives the date context, but its small numerals and two marked days dilute the deadline.
The underlined “in Studio” explains membership in one line. The long path wraps and competes with a second band of small type in the weekly calendar.
The folder tab holds the full path and the separate “17h overdue” callout clearly identifies urgency. The callout has less editing affordance than the project chevron.
“Filed in” and “Move…” clearly belong together, but the two ruled sections and the week of dates below them make the deadline slower to locate in the overdue state.
The dotted deadline line and project chevron give separate interaction cues. The right-hand date forces a three-line title, and the project initial can resemble an assignee.
The enclosing folder tab and October date tile give the two fields distinct shapes. The tile's small month and lack of a disclosure cue weaken its role as a control.
A folder breadcrumb and dotted deadline underline distinguish the controls. The breadcrumb wraps above a three-line title and the due time sits directly opposite the scheduled time.
“in Studio” and its underline make membership and editing legible. The deadline column narrows the title and places two clock times across the same title block.
The folder breadcrumb gives project context before the title. The overdue date appears twice in the week strip, where tiny day labels and two highlighted dates slow scanning.
“Filed in” and “Move…” give the project its own action, and the dotted line singles out the date. Keeping that date beside the title costs an extra line of title text.
“Filed in” and “Due in 26h” explicitly identify the two values. “Move…” is an obvious project action, while the deadline immediately below it looks read-only once set.
The countdown cleanly differentiates due time from 10 AM. The initial badge and chevron look interactive, but Studio alone offers less evidence that it names a project.
A split footer groups the folder and flag into stable separate cells. The dot-separated project path is hard to parse and “Add date” leaves the date's purpose implicit.
Two full-width rows with chevrons give each field an obvious action. A flag and red type are the only evidence that “Oct 15 · 4:30 PM” is overdue.
“in Studio” establishes membership and the separate calendar tile draws the eye to the deadline. The project looks like a link while the existing deadline looks like a display.
The folder tab fits the long path and the dotted line marks the right-hand date. That date column reduces title width and offers only “Yesterday” and a time in the overdue state.
The folder and chevron place Studio above the title, while the lower date tile separates noon from 10 AM. The tile has no visible edit cue once filled.
“in Studio” and “Due in 26h” explain both roles. The underlined project could open Studio, and the ruled countdown looks like a status display.
The underlined project and dotted deadline are distinguishable, but putting the deadline opposite 10 AM narrows the title to three lines and leaves the flag to explain which time is due.
The project menu highlights the leaf above its parent path, but its initial resembles an assignee avatar. The large day numeral is easier to find than the small time beside it.
The initial badge and arrow suggest a selector without identifying what Studio is. The dotted flag field is compact but crowds the title and sits level with the scheduled time.
The folder breadcrumb gives the project a clear home. The week strip highlights a day but leaves two circles and seven tiny numbers to interpret below the task.
The folder tab contains the whole project path on one line, and “17h overdue” is independent of the scheduled time. The tab looks editable while the countdown resembles a readout.
“Filed in” and “Move…” make membership and reassignment explicit. The nearby countdown identifies the deadline precisely but has a weaker edit cue than Move.
“in Studio” reads naturally under the task and the date tile stands apart from 10 AM. The link could navigate to the project and the tile could be static.
The folder tab gives even the long path one line, but the weekday strip repeats the date below the flag and makes a set deadline take much more space than an empty one.
The footer divider groups two distinct hit areas away from the schedule and tags. “Add date” is vague and the dotted project path wraps without a strong hierarchy cue.
The project arrow and selected calendar day offer separate interaction cues. An initial badge can suggest a person, and the seven-day strip competes with the task for attention.
The filing row explicitly offers to move the task. The dotted deadline is easy to locate but squeezes the title and relies on its flag to differentiate noon from the scheduled time.
The folder path above and explicit due or overdue text below distinguish both roles from tags and schedule. Only the project carries a persistent menu arrow.
The tab clearly frames the task by project, including the long path. The right-side date has a dotted edit cue but its narrow column wraps the empty action and the title.
The filing row names the relationship and exposes Move. The dated tile sits apart from the schedule, but lacks a comparable edit cue and makes a second footer tier.
“Due in 26h” is unambiguous even beside a scheduled task, but the project initial can suggest an assignee until a parent path or “Choose project” appears.
The filing command makes project editing explicit. A separate row of seven small dates under it pushes the deadline time to the far right and makes the bottom of the card dense.
The tab places the whole task inside its project and the large day tile stands apart from the tags and schedule. Editing a set date is less obvious than opening the tab.
The project reads as a location under the title, but a wrapped link and seven-day strip make the overdue card busy. The strip can read as a scheduling calendar.
Folder and dotted flag distinguish the fields, but the long breadcrumb wraps above a three-line title and places two different times on the same horizontal band.
Two full-width rows with separate chevrons clearly offer independent editing. The dotted project path is harder to parse and the flag alone identifies the second row as a deadline.
The folder tab makes the entire card feel filed under Studio. The seven-day strip requires distinguishing the outlined 16 from the filled 17 to read the deadline visually.
The breadcrumb sits directly above the task and the calendar tile separates noon from the scheduled 10 AM. The populated date has no equivalent to the project's disclosure arrow.
“in Studio” reads naturally below the title and “Due in 26h” identifies noon explicitly. The underlined path and exact timestamp both use small secondary text.
“Filed in” and “Move…” explain membership and editing. The separate week below adds seven dates to inspect and makes the overdue card substantially taller.
The underlined “in Studio” and large 17 serve different purposes at a glance. The date tile looks more like a calendar illustration than a date-editing control.
Folder and disclosure mark the project, while a dotted underline marks the trailing date. That date shares a band with 10 AM and forces the title onto three lines.
The bold project leaf and arrow remain easy to find above the note. Its initial badge resembles an assignee avatar until the parent path or “Choose project” is visible.
The folder tab contains the complete long path and the large numeral anchors the deadline away from 10 AM. The calendar tile gives less indication of editing than the tab's arrow.
Folder, path and explicit “Due in 26h” distinguish both fields, including when overdue. The vertical rule makes the populated deadline resemble a status annotation.
The folder tab gives the long project its own full-width line. The dotted date is visibly separate but “Set due date” wraps beside a three-line task title.
A folder tab identifies where the whole card belongs, and “17h overdue” identifies the lower time explicitly. The small exact date sits inside a readout with no disclosure cue.
The project arrow and explicit “Due in” text are easy to locate separately. The letter badge identifies neither filing nor hierarchy on a task with a one-word project.
Project initials and parentage occupy a separate row and the lower strip shows the due week. The several date markers and letter badge demand interpretation on the same card.
Underlining makes the project and date look independently editable. The trailing deadline narrows both title and underlined path and sits level with the scheduled hour.
The calendar tile isolates the deadline from the scheduled time and “Move…” names the filing action. The filled tile offers little indication that its value can also change.
Two full-width rows with individual disclosures are clearly separate actions. “Add date” omits its due purpose, and the dot-delimited project path is hard to parse.
The folder breadcrumb identifies the project's hierarchy above the title. The deadline adds a full calendar strip below the note, with today and due day both marked.
The badge has a project dropdown and the trailing deadline has a distinct dotted underline. A one-letter avatar and two times level with the title leave their meanings less immediate.
“Filed in,” “Move…” and “Due in 26h” identify the roles explicitly. The ruled countdown reads as informational beside the much more actionable filing button.
A split footer makes the fields quick to find and leaves title width intact. Its shared background and lack of disclosures make two independent edit actions less apparent once both values are set.
“Filed in” and “Move…” explain project placement. The flagged trailing time has an edit cue but shares the title band with 10 AM and lacks an absolute date when overdue.
“in” identifies the linked project even when it wraps. The compact exact deadline must compete with a ruled calendar that shows two different marked days.
The folder tab frames the whole task and the flagged date stays opposite 10:00 AM, clear of the tags. The dotted underline suggests editing, though the small empty “Set due date” wraps.

The folder tab establishes belonging and the calendar tile draws the eye to the bottom-right deadline. The future tile repeats Oct 29 beside it, and the filled date has a weaker editing cue than the project chevron.

The breadcrumb directly above the title makes even the long project readable. The flagged week strip separates due time from 10:00 AM but introduces seven tiny dates to scan and leaves the editing target ambiguous.

Two full-width rows with separate chevrons make editing easy to discover. The folder is distinct from the tags, but “Add date” is ambiguous and the due-today row gives only the absolute date and time.

The divided footer keeps the folder and flag together and apart from scheduled time. The split implies separate fields, but filled values look passive, the long project uses literal dots, and “Add date” leaves its purpose implicit.

The folder tab frames the task while “Due in 6h” and “17h overdue” explicitly identify the separate deadline, with exact timing below. The empty date looks actionable, but the filled colored rule reads like a status indicator.

The folder tab and breadcrumb show where the task belongs. The flagged Today or Yesterday sits opposite 10 AM, clear of the tags. The dotted underline is a subtler edit cue than the project chevron, and Set due date wraps.

Separate folder and flag rows each have a chevron, making both edits easy to find. Add date leaves its purpose vague, Oct 16 does not announce Today, and the long dotted project path is harder to parse.

The folder tab anchors the task and the calendar tile makes the deadline easy to find away from 10 AM and tags. The future date appears twice, and the filled tile looks more like a calendar badge than an edit control.

The divided footer keeps folder and flag together and clear of the schedule and tags. The long dotted path fits, but the divider alone signals two targets, and Add date leaves the kind of date implicit.

The folder breadcrumb conveys membership. Due in 6h and 17h overdue identify the deadline even without color, with the exact time beneath. The filled deadline reads like a status readout despite the explicit Set due date action when empty.

The chevron and breadcrumb above the title make project membership clear. The weekday strip competes with the flagged deadline, repeats the future date, and shows two marked days in the overdue state, obscuring where to tap to edit.

The folder tab and breadcrumb identify the project above the title. The separate flag and calendar distinguish the deadline from 10:00 AM, though Oct 29 appears twice and the filled date has no edit cue.

The folder tab makes project selection clear. Due in 6h over Oct 16 · 4 PM explicitly identifies the deadline alongside the scheduled 10:00 AM. The thin colored rule makes the filled deadline look like a status readout.

The folder breadcrumb and chevron clearly locate the task. The week strip draws attention away from the title, uses small weekday initials, and marks both 15 and 16 in the overdue state. Set due date is clearer than the filled strip about what tapping changes.

The divided footer groups two distinct values away from the tags and scheduled time. Add project and Add date expose both actions when empty. Filled cells lose those cues, and the long dot-separated project reads as one string.

Separate full-width rows with trailing chevrons make both edits easy to find in every state. The due-today row shows Oct 16 · 4 PM without a Today cue, and the long project name relies on periods to convey hierarchy.

The folder tab frames the title and the right-aligned flag distinguishes the deadline from the scheduled time on the left. The dotted underline suggests editing, though the narrow deadline column wraps Set due date and reduces title space.
